name: AD8021ARZ-REEL
title: AD8021: low-noise, high-speed voltage-feedback op amp with external compensation and output disable, SOIC-8 and MSOP-8
summary: A single voltage-feedback operational amplifier built for 16-bit signal chains: 2.1 nV/√Hz and 2.1 pA/√Hz input noise at 7 mA supply current on ±5 V. A capacitor from the CCOMP pin to the negative rail sets the compensation, so bandwidth can be held near 150 to 490 MHz from a gain of 1 to a gain of 10 instead of falling with gain. It runs from ±2.25 V to ±12 V or a single 5 V supply, settles to 0.01 % in 23 ns, and has a DISABLE pin, referred to its own LOGIC REFERENCE pin, that cuts supply current to 1.3 mA. Offered in 8-lead SOIC and MSOP for −40 °C to +85 °C.
key_figures: 2.1 nV/√Hz typ, 2.6 nV/√Hz max at 50 kHz
490 MHz at G = +1 (CC = 10 pF); 150 MHz at G = +10 (CC = 0 pF)

The electrical tables cover the SOIC (AD8021AR) and MSOP (AD8021ARM) versions alike.

pins.name: LOGIC REFERENCE
pins.function: Reference level for the DISABLE pin; connect it to the low rail of the logic that drives DISABLE.

pins.name: CCOMP
pins.function: Compensation node: the external capacitor CC goes from this pin to −VS. Its value depends on the noise gain (Table 6, Figure 59).

pins.name: DISABLE
pins.function: Active-low disable. The amplifier runs while this pin sits about 2 V or more above LOGIC REFERENCE and shuts off when it comes within about 1.5 V of it. With pins 1 and 8 both unconnected the amplifier is on.

operation.text: Inside, the amplifier carries only about 1.5 pF of compensation; the capacitor CC from CCOMP (pin 5) to −VS adds the rest. When the compensation is fixed on chip, a voltage-feedback amp trades bandwidth for gain one for one; with the AD8021, CC is chosen for the noise gain, so the closed-loop bandwidth stays high from G = 1 to G = 10. In a simplified open-loop picture (Figure 58), G = +1 with CC = 10 pF gives about 200 MHz and 60° of phase margin; moving to G = +10 with CC still 10 pF drops to about 20 MHz and 90°, and cutting CC to 0 pF restores about 200 MHz and 60°. Slew rate goes roughly as 1/CC. CC follows the noise gain, not the signal gain (Table 6, Figure 59).

A smaller CC widens the bandwidth and raises peaking as phase margin falls (Figure 7); a larger CC adds margin and narrows the bandwidth. Input capacitance, of the part and the board, acting with RF eats phase margin (Figure 14); a capacitor CF across RF compensates for it. Source-side series resistance and the input capacitance together form a pole and damp resonances from package and board parasitics (Figure 15). Larger resistors add noise; a smaller RF loads the output harder and raises distortion (Figure 22).

DISABLE (pin 8) works against LOGIC REFERENCE (pin 1). With DISABLE about 2 V or more above pin 1 the amplifier is on; pulled to less than about 1.5 V above pin 1 it turns off and supply current drops to 1.3 mA typ at ±5 V. The exact thresholds are the DISABLE voltage rows of Tables 1 to 3. When the feature is not wanted, tie DISABLE to the positive supply or a logic high and LOGIC REFERENCE to ground or logic low, or leave both pins open: the part is then on.

The part is made on a complementary bipolar process (XFCB) whose NPN and PNP transistors both reach fT near 3 GHz and are dielectrically isolated, which removes junction-isolation parasitics and latch-up and lowers nonlinear capacitance. Supply current is trimmed, so bandwidth, slew rate, distortion and settling vary little from part to part. The input is an NPN differential pair at 0.8 mA per transistor, which gives the low voltage noise; it feeds a PNP folded cascode and a current mirror that turn the differential signal into a single-ended current into the high-impedance node at pin 5, where CC sits. The output stage buffers that node with a current gain of 5000, so open-loop gain holds up into heavy loads.

Two diodes clamp across the inputs (pins 2 and 3) to keep large differential voltages from breaking down the input transistors' emitter-base junctions, which would degrade offset and bias current. There are no internal series resistors, to keep noise down, so beyond ±0.8 V of differential input the input current must be limited to ±10 mA externally.

The junction limit for the plastic package is about 150 °C, set by the glass transition of the mold compound; running above 175 °C for long can destroy the part. The output is short-circuit protected, but that alone does not keep the junction under 150 °C, so dissipation must stay within the derating curve of Figure 3 (θJA 125 °C/W for SOIC, 145 °C/W for MSOP, in free air).

Keep the leads short between the bypass capacitors' grounds and between CC and −VS; stray inductance there shapes the frequency response and can make the part oscillate. A multilayer board with an inner ground plane lowers ground noise and allows a compact layout. Because pin 5 is a high-impedance node and CC is small, ring pin 5 with a guard trace tied to the output (pin 6), which sits at nearly the same potential: it shields the node from nearby noise and cuts stray capacitance that would lower bandwidth. Place CC right at the package edge across pins 4 and 5, as a surface-mount C0G/NPO ceramic, not a leaded part, and place the high-frequency bypass capacitors right at pins 4 and 7. RF can sit under the board, spanning pin 6 to pin 2 for the shortest inverting-input lead, and the ground end of RG should land close to the ground end of the −VS bypass capacitor (Figure 62).

Harmonic distortion stays better than −90 dBc from 100 kHz to 1 MHz (Figure 19), and the extra loop gain from tailored compensation steadies the output and lowers noise when the converter's input switches during a sample. Figure 63 (inverting, gain −7.5, 10 V p-p at 65 kHz) and Figure 64 (noninverting, gain 10.1, about 20 V p-p at 100 kHz, no filtering) drive an AD7665; Tables 7 and 8 give the measured distortion.

Built from two fixed-compensation amplifiers, an inverter and a follower at the same gain do not match: the inverter's higher noise gain gives it less bandwidth (Figure 66). Giving the inverter a smaller CCOMP lifts its bandwidth to the follower's, and the two responses then match closely (Figure 67). In Figure 65 the feedback and load resistors keep the total load under 1 kΩ, and the resistances seen at each amplifier's inputs are matched to hold down offset voltage and drift.

A real low-pass filter's stop-band attenuation is limited by the op amp's gain bandwidth, and its pass band by the op amp's noise and DC gain. Figure 68 with Table 9 is a two-pole low-pass with a Bessel-type response at gains of 2 and 5; Figure 69 is its measured response.

A capacitive load makes the response peak ahead of its roll-off. There are two remedies: raise CC, which cuts the peaking while keeping the low-frequency gain flat, or put a resistor RSNUB between VOUT and the load. Figure 70 shows both on a 33 pF load; Figure 71 gives the RSNUB that holds peaking to 2 dB at G = +2 for loads up to about 48 pF. RSNUB costs some low-frequency gain (equation above).
